prompt: Define RAII in one sentence and name three resources it manages besides heap memory.
reveal: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): bind a resource’s lifetime to an object’s lifetime — acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor — so cleanup is automatic and exception-safe. Besides heap memory: file handles (std::fstream), locks (std::lock_guard), sockets, database connections, GPU buffers.

prompt: What does std::move actually do, and why can a std::vector be moved in O(1) but copied in O(n)?
reveal: std::move is just a cast to an rvalue reference — it moves nothing itself; it marks an object as eligible to be moved from. A vector move copies only its three members (data pointer, size, capacity) and nulls the source, so the heap buffer is transferred, not duplicated — O(1). A copy must allocate a new buffer and copy every element — O(n). This is why unique_ptr is movable but not copyable: transferring sole ownership makes sense; duplicating it does not.

prompt: unique_ptr vs shared_ptr vs weak_ptr: when each, and what problem does weak_ptr solve?
reveal: unique_ptr = single exclusive owner, zero overhead vs a raw pointer — your default. shared_ptr = shared ownership via an atomic reference count; the object dies when the count hits zero (use only when ownership is genuinely shared — counting costs). weak_ptr = a non-owning observer of a shared_ptr that doesn’t keep it alive; it breaks reference cycles (two shared_ptrs pointing at each other would never reach count zero — a leak). You lock() a weak_ptr to get a shared_ptr if the object still exists.

prompt: State the Rule of Zero and why it’s preferred over the Rule of Five.

src.ref: C.20 (Rule of Zero) / C.21 (Rule of Five)

reveal: Rule of Zero: design classes so they need NO user-declared destructor, copy/move constructor, or copy/move assignment — by holding resources in types that already manage themselves (smart pointers, containers). Then the compiler-generated special members are correct. It’s preferred because hand-written special members are error-prone; if you must write one (Rule of Five says write all five), you’re usually better off wrapping the raw resource in an RAII type instead.

prompt: How does a virtual function call work under the hood (vtable/vptr), and what is its cost vs a normal call?

src.ref: C.67 & the object model; see also bare-metal C++ on avoiding it

reveal: Each polymorphic class has a vtable (array of function pointers); each object holds a hidden vptr to its class’s vtable. A virtual call dereferences the vptr, indexes the vtable, and calls through the pointer — one extra indirection, and it usually can’t be inlined, which is the bigger cost. In hot or bare-metal code you often prefer compile-time polymorphism (templates/CRTP) to get the abstraction with zero runtime dispatch and no vtable.

prompt: On a bare-metal target with no heap and exceptions disabled, how do you get polymorphism and dynamic-like behavior? What must you avoid from the STL?

src.ref: Practical Guide to Bare-metal C++ — Compile-Time Polymorphism & Dynamic Memory

reveal: Use compile-time polymorphism — templates and CRTP — so dispatch is resolved at compile time with zero runtime cost and no vtable/heap. Avoid STL facilities that allocate (std::vector, std::string, std::map) or that rely on exceptions/RTTI; prefer fixed-capacity containers, std::array, and static storage. Wrap hardware registers in typed volatile abstractions. The book’s thesis: modern C++ abstractions cost nothing at runtime if you push them to compile time.

prompt: Explain struct padding and alignment. Why can reordering fields shrink a struct, and how does this interact with cache lines?

src.ref: CSAPP §3.9 (data alignment); C++ Core Guidelines on layout

reveal: The compiler inserts padding so each field sits at an address that is a multiple of its size (alignment), which the hardware requires or strongly prefers. A small field followed by a larger one forces padding; ordering fields largest-to-smallest minimizes the holes, shrinking the struct. Smaller, well-packed structs fit more per 64-byte cache line, so traversals pull in more useful data per fetch — layout is a cache decision.

prompt: What is perfect forwarding? Explain reference collapsing and why std::forward is not std::move.
reveal: Perfect forwarding preserves an argument’s value category (lvalue/rvalue) and constness when passing it through a template wrapper. It relies on a FORWARDING reference T&& in a deduced context, plus reference collapsing: T& && collapses to T&, T&& && collapses to T&&. std::forward<T>(x) casts to T&& only when T was deduced as an rvalue, so lvalues stay lvalues — whereas std::move unconditionally casts to rvalue, which would steal from an lvalue the caller still owns. Rule: std::move for things you know are expiring, std::forward only inside templates on forwarding references.

prompt: What are RVO and copy elision, and what does C++17 guarantee? Does returning std::move(x) help?
reveal: Copy elision lets the compiler construct the returned object directly in the caller’s storage, skipping copy/move entirely. Since C++17, elision is GUARANTEED for prvalues (returning a temporary such as return Foo(...)), so no copy or move constructor need even exist. Named RVO (returning a local variable) is still optional but implemented by every real compiler. Returning std::move(x) is actively HARMFUL: it turns the expression into an xvalue, disabling NRVO and forcing a move that would otherwise have been elided entirely.

prompt: Iterator invalidation: state the rules for vector, deque, list, and unordered_map.
reveal: vector: any reallocation (push_back beyond capacity, resize, reserve) invalidates ALL iterators, pointers, and references; erase invalidates everything at or after the erased position. deque: insertion at either END invalidates iterators but NOT references to elements; insertion in the middle invalidates everything. list/forward_list: only iterators to the erased element are invalidated — everything else survives, which is the reason to choose it. unordered_map: rehashing (on insert past max_load_factor) invalidates iterators but NOT references/pointers to elements; erase invalidates only the erased element.

prompt: vector vs deque vs list: give the one-line reason to pick each.
reveal: vector — the default: contiguous memory, cache-friendly traversal, O(1) random access, amortized O(1) push_back. deque — when you need O(1) insertion at BOTH ends and stable references to existing elements, at the cost of a two-level indirection and worse traversal locality. list — rarely correct in modern C++; only when you need O(1) splice or guaranteed reference/iterator stability across arbitrary insertions and deletions. Even for frequent middle-insertion, vector often wins because memmove on contiguous data beats pointer chasing.

prompt: What is CRTP, what problem does it solve, and what are its limits?
reveal: The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern: class Derived : public Base<Derived>, so the base knows its derived type at COMPILE time and can static_cast<Derived*>(this) to call derived methods. It gives you polymorphic-looking code with zero runtime cost — no vtable, no indirect call, full inlining — which is why it appears in hot paths and bare-metal code. Limits: it is static, so you cannot store heterogeneous CRTP types in one container or choose the implementation at runtime; every instantiation generates separate code (binary bloat); and error messages are notoriously bad. C++20 concepts cover much of the same ground more readably.

prompt: What is PIMPL, what does it buy, and what does it cost?
reveal: PIMPL (pointer to implementation) moves a class’s private members into a forward-declared struct held via a unique_ptr, so the header exposes only the public interface. It buys COMPILATION FIREWALL (changing private members does not recompile every translation unit that includes the header) and stable ABI (member layout changes do not break callers). Costs: an extra heap allocation per object, an indirection on every member access (bad for hot paths), and the destructor must be defined in the .cpp where Impl is complete — otherwise unique_ptr fails to compile on the incomplete type.

prompt: What are the exception safety guarantees, and what does the copy-and-swap idiom achieve?
reveal: Four levels: NO-THROW (never fails — required of destructors and swap), STRONG (if it throws, the program state is unchanged — commit-or-rollback), BASIC (no leaks, invariants intact, but state may have changed), and NONE. Copy-and-swap achieves the STRONG guarantee for assignment: construct a complete copy first (any throw happens here, before you have touched *this), then swap it with *this using a no-throw swap; the old state dies with the temporary. It also gives you self-assignment safety and unifies copy and move assignment into one function.

prompt: What does const mean on a member function, and what is the difference between logical and bitwise constness? Where does mutable fit?

src.ref: Con.2 Member functions should be const by default

reveal: A const member function promises not to modify the observable state; the compiler enforces BITWISE constness — it forbids modifying any non-static data member. LOGICAL constness is the weaker, semantic notion: the object appears unchanged to callers even if some internal bookkeeping changes. mutable bridges them: a mutable member can be modified inside a const function, which is legitimate for caches, memoization, and mutexes (locking a mutex in a const getter is the canonical example). Note const does NOT imply thread safety, but the standard library assumes const operations are safe to call concurrently.

prompt: Name five common sources of undefined behavior in C++, and explain why UB is worse than a wrong answer.
reveal: Signed integer overflow; out-of-bounds array or container access; dereferencing null or dangling pointers; reading an uninitialized variable; data races; and violating strict aliasing (reading an object through an incompatible type). UB is worse than a wrong answer because the compiler is allowed to ASSUME it never happens and optimize accordingly — so a null check after a dereference may be deleted entirely, or a loop with signed overflow may be assumed infinite. The bug can manifest arbitrarily far from its cause, appear only under optimization, and change behavior between compilers.

prompt: How does a lambda capture work under the hood? Contrast [=], [&], and [this], and name the dangling trap.
reveal: A lambda is syntactic sugar for a compiler-generated closure class with an operator(); captures become its data members. [=] copies each used variable into the closure; [&] stores references; [this] captures the raw this POINTER (not the object), so members are accessed through it. The dangling trap: any lambda that outlives its enclosing scope while holding [&] captures — or [this] after the object is destroyed — reads freed memory. This is common with lambdas stored in a thread pool or std::function. Prefer capturing by value for escaping lambdas, and use [*this] (C++17) to copy the object.

prompt: What does constexpr guarantee, and how does consteval differ? Why does this matter for performance work?
reveal: constexpr means a function or variable CAN be evaluated at compile time given constant arguments — it may still run at runtime otherwise. consteval (C++20) means it MUST be evaluated at compile time; a runtime call is a compile error. constinit guarantees static initialization, eliminating the static-initialization-order fiasco. It matters for performance because work moved to compile time costs zero at runtime — lookup tables, dispatch tables, and unit conversions can be fully baked in, which is exactly the bare-metal and HFT philosophy of pushing abstraction to compile time.

prompt: What are SFINAE and concepts? Show the shape of constraining a template both ways.
reveal: SFINAE (Substitution Failure Is Not An Error) means an invalid substitution during template deduction silently removes that overload from consideration rather than being an error — exploited through std::enable_if_t<condition, T> in a return type or extra parameter to enable/disable overloads. It works but is unreadable and produces enormous errors. C++20 concepts replace it: template<std::integral T> void f(T), or requires-clauses, which express the same constraints declaratively, give clear diagnostics at the point of failure, and participate in overload resolution ordering (more constrained wins).

prompt: What is the difference between public, protected, and private inheritance, and when is composition better?
reveal: public inheritance models IS-A: the derived type is substitutable for the base (Liskov). protected exposes base members to further derived classes only. private inheritance models IMPLEMENTED-IN-TERMS-OF — no substitutability — and is essentially composition with the ability to override virtuals or exploit the empty base optimization. Composition is better in nearly every case that is not a genuine IS-A: it is looser coupling, testable, and avoids fragile-base-class problems. The Core Guidelines rule of thumb: use inheritance for interfaces and polymorphism, composition for reuse.

prompt: Why must a polymorphic base class have a virtual destructor? What exactly happens if it does not?

src.ref: C.35 A base class destructor should be either public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual

reveal: If you delete a derived object through a base pointer and the base destructor is non-virtual, the behavior is UNDEFINED — in practice only the base destructor runs, so the derived part is never destroyed and its resources leak. Making it virtual routes the destruction through the vtable to the correct derived destructor, which then chains up. The alternative the guidelines offer: if the class is not meant to be deleted polymorphically, make the destructor protected and non-virtual, which makes such deletion a compile error.

prompt: What is the small-string / small-buffer optimization and why does it matter for latency-sensitive code?
reveal: SSO stores short strings directly inside the string object’s own storage (typically up to 15–22 bytes depending on implementation) instead of heap-allocating. It matters because a heap allocation is orders of magnitude more expensive than a stack write, and it introduces allocator contention across threads plus unpredictable latency spikes — unacceptable in a hot loop. The same idea appears in std::function (small callables stored inline) and in custom containers. In latency work, the general principle is to know exactly where allocations happen and eliminate them from the critical path.

prompt: What do alignof and alignas do, and give a concrete case where alignment changes performance rather than correctness.

src.ref: Layout and alignment; hardware interference size

reveal: alignof reports the required alignment of a type; alignas requests a stricter one. Correctness matters for SIMD types (some instructions fault or slow down on unaligned data) and hardware registers. The performance case is FALSE SHARING: two atomics used by different threads landing on the same 64-byte cache line will ping-pong between cores, so you write alignas(64) (or std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) to give each its own line. The inverse, hardware_constructive_interference_size, is used to deliberately pack data you want fetched together.
